83l69u.title: Investigate other methods of identification
83l69u.body:
We need to investiagate other auth methods such as a list of trusted domains so that external events such as
Webhooks can be processed without requiring API Keys
S-20: fetch as any — the property is stored as []string by
ContextWithClaims and as []any by some producers, and asserting
[]any directly failed the type check for the former, silently
skipping the gate (allow-all) for exactly the scoped keys it

8uuufn.title: Cleaun up old manual code
8uuufn.body:
uncleaned implementations. We should probably clean them up
by first consolidating all hand rolled models with the generated
model and secondly prefering autogenerated code
Converted all fmt.Errorf calls in auth/ to common.SystemError: service.go (10), credential_provider.go (7), session_service.go (8), seed.go (5). No duplicate implementations remain.

arch-20260821-003.title: Duplicated identity property extraction pattern
arch-20260821-003.body:
The pattern `ident.Properties.(map[string]any)` followed by key extraction
appears in 8+ places across 5 files:

1. secure-dispatcher.go:66,127
2. rate-limit.go:132,145
3. throttle.go:46
4. access-log-dispatcher.go:89
5. core/interface/http/middleware.go:144

This is a mechanical pattern that should be a shared helper. The existing
devnotes #review-20260821-006 and #review-20260821-007 call for a helper
like `GetIdentityProperty[T](ctx, key)` or a typed `IdentityProperties` struct.

Resolution: Create a `runtime/identity` helper package with generic functions
like `GetProperty[T](ctx, key) (T, bool)` to eliminate all copies.

arch-20260821-004.title: Separate rate store instances per dispatcher
arch-20260821-004.body:
RateLimitDispatcher creates its own ratestore.New() instance at line 61.
ThrottleDispatcher (throttle.go:78) creates a separate ratestore.New() instance.

Each dispatcher creates an independent InMemoryStore instance with its own
eviction goroutine and shard array. This doubles memory usage and means
rate limits and throttles are tracked in separate stores even when they
could share infrastructure.

Resolution: Pass the RateLimitStore via DI or constructor instead of creating
new instances internally in each dispatcher. This allows sharing a single
store instance across dispatchers.

arch-20260821-005.title: Inconsistent error handling in dispatchers
arch-20260821-005.body:
LocalDispatcher.Send uses fmt.Errorf for handler-not-found and disabled errors,
but the project convention is to use common.SystemError for consistency with
the rest of the codebase (see core/runtime/errors.go).

The same issue exists in bootstrap-dispatcher.go.

Meanwhile, secure-dispatcher.go and rate-limit.go correctly use ErrAccessDenied,
ErrAuthRequired, ErrRateLimited etc.

Resolution: Replace all fmt.Errorf handler-dispatch errors in local-dispatcher.go
and bootstrap-dispatcher.go with appropriate SystemError sentinels (ErrNotFound,
ErrValidation/ErrAccessDenied with WithOperation).

arch-20260821-008.title: Subpackage imports parent runtime package
arch-20260821-008.body:
notification/channel_email.go imports its own parent runtime package (for *runtime.Mailer).
This violates expected hierarchical dependency direction — subpackages should not import
their parent.

The Mailer type (or its interface) should live in a shared location like:
- A new `core/config` package (alongside other config types)
- The `abstract` package (as an interface)
- A dedicated `core/mailer` package

Resolution: Extract a Mailer interface in abstract or the new config package
so notification does not need to import runtime.

arch-20260821-009.title: Hardcoded HTML template in Go source
arch-20260821-009.body:
The password reset email HTML template is a fmt.Sprintf string literal
(mailer.go:89-98). This makes it difficult to maintain, test, and internationalize.

The existing TODO at line 83 acknowledges this issue.

Resolution: Move templates to a templates/ directory with .html files,
use Go's html/template package for rendering, support i18n for different
locales, and make the template configurable per deployment.

arch-20260821-010.title: Race condition in AuditBuffer circuit breaker
arch-20260821-010.body:
The Write method (line 63) reads b.failed under mutex, then calls wg.Add(1)
outside the lock. A concurrent Close() could interleave between the check
and the wg.Add(1).

Additionally, on re-enqueue failure (line 121-125), wg.Done() is called
without guaranteeing it was incremented for this entry. This could cause
a panic if the entry was never added to the WaitGroup.

The circuit breaker is only reset on successful persist in flushLoop,
but if the buffer is full and the circuit opens, entries are dropped
permanently until a successful persist occurs. Consider adding a
timeout-based circuit breaker reset or a maximum drop count before recovery.

Resolution: Hold the mutex across the entire check-and-add sequence,
or use an atomic flag. Ensure wg.Done() is only called when wg.Add(1)
was successfully called for the same entry.

arch-20260821-011.title: Scheduler jobs have no lifecycle context
arch-20260821-011.body:
The Register method wraps the job function with context.Background() (line 51),
which means scheduled jobs have no access to the application's lifecycle context.

This could be problematic for:
1. Graceful shutdown - jobs can't be cancelled
2. Tracing - jobs can't be linked to the parent trace
3. Timeout control - jobs run indefinitely

Resolution: Store the context passed to Start() and use it for job execution,
or accept a context factory function at registration time.

arch-20260821-013.title: Domain types in leaf package
arch-20260821-013.body:
runtime is a leaf package but contains domain types that other packages depend on:

- Policy types (RateLimitPolicy, ThrottlePolicy, ThrottleActionPolicy) - stored
  in the _operation_policy_ collection alongside each operation
- Rate limit types (RateLimitError, RateLimitStore, MatchIdentity, RateLimitLookup)
- Capability types (CapabilityItem, CapabilitiesDocument)
- Permission types (PermissionManager, ReloadablePermissionManager, CapabilityMetadata)
- Metadata types (RateLimitMeta)
- Audit context keys (AuditActorIDKey, etc.)

These types are used extensively throughout the codebase (52+ files import runtime).
This creates a tight coupling between the runtime package and all other packages.

Resolution: Move domain types to proper packages:
- RateLimitPolicy/ThrottlePolicy -> operations/policy or similar model package
- PermissionManager -> permissions package
- RateLimitStore -> ratestore package
- CapabilityItem/CapabilitiesDocument -> capabilities package

arch-20260821-014.title: Lock ordering inconsistency in ratestore
arch-20260821-014.body:
The evictStale method (line 150) acquires shard.mu and then bucket.mu,
while other methods (CheckAndConsume, Increment) acquire bucket.mu first.

This lock ordering inconsistency could lead to deadlocks if concurrent
operations are happening. For example:
- Thread A: evictStale holds shard.mu, waits for bucket.mu
- Thread B: CheckAndConsume holds bucket.mu, waits for shard.mu

Resolution: Use a consistent lock ordering throughout, or use a different
eviction strategy that doesn't require holding both locks simultaneously.

auth-20261029-001.title: No route returns the current session's claims (blocks multi-tab restore)
auth-20261029-001.body:
Resolved: added system:auth:session:get (GetSession) returning the sanitized user and absolute expires_at, gated by the authenticated rule.

The session cookie is HttpOnly, so page JS cannot read it and a fresh tab
has no way to learn that a valid session already exists. Today:
  - system:auth:session:validate is Internal and wants a raw token in the
    request body, which a browser does not have;
  - it returns only ids and timestamps, no email or permissions;
  - system:core:heartbeat returns nothing;
  - system:users:user:get needs a user id the new tab does not have.

Proposal: add system:auth:session:get (intent=read, rule=authenticated, not
internal) returning the same sanitized user document CreateSession builds,
plus expires_at (absolute session expiry, unix seconds). authMiddleware
already puts expires_at and token_id into the resolved identity properties,
so the handler is: read claims from ctx, load the user, sanitize with the
"users" scope, return. Do NOT list it in NoRefreshCommands: like every other
authenticated request it should slide the cookie.

auth-20261029-002.title: Login response carries no session expiry
auth-20261029-002.body:
Resolved: CreateSession now captures SessionInfo.ExpiresAt and emits expires_at on the login document; LoginResult.expires_at exposes it to clients.

LoginOutput holds only the user. The absolute expiry (now + sessionTTL,
DefaultSessionTTL = 8h) lives only inside the cookie, so clients guess it
(IAM consumers hard-code 8h) and drift from the server. Return expires_at
(unix seconds) from CreateSession, and from session:get (#auth-20261029-001).
The client maps it onto IAM's per-login session.ttl override.

auth-20261029-003.title: HestiaAuth has no session()/restore call
auth-20261029-003.body:
Resolved: HestiaAuth.session() dispatches system:auth:session:get with notifyAuthStateChange:false; 401 clears identity and returns null, other errors throw. resume() was removed.

A resume() stub now exists below, but it throws "Method not implemented", so
the capability is still missing. Proposal: session(): Promise<LoginResult | null>.
  - dispatches system:auth:session:get with notifyAuthStateChange:false so a
    "not logged in" answer does not run the global 401 handler;
  - 200: setIdentity(user) and return { user, expires_at };
  - 401: clear the local identity and return null;
  - anything else (network error, 5xx): THROW. Callers must be able to tell
    "not logged in" from "could not check", or an offline blip logs users out.
LoginResult gains expires_at?: number (see #auth-20261029-002). Either
implement resume() on top of session() or replace it outright.

auth-20261029-004.title: @asaidimu/iam 8.2.0 cannot adopt an existing server session
auth-20261029-004.body:
Resolved: the reference integration now targets @asaidimu/iam 9.x and uses onRestore to adopt the cookie-backed session.
To be filed in asaidimu/iam (all verified by reading 8.2.0):
  1. No startup hook can supply an identity. onVerify only runs when an
     identity is already persisted; onLoad is undocumented, ignores its
     boolean result and cannot provide an identity.
  2. provider.refresh() returns null when there is no identity, so refresh()
     cannot restore a session.
  3. onVerify/onLoad are typed Identity | null but onVerify is only called
     with non-null; onLoad(null) fires twice on a failed verify.
  4. config.persistence is ignored when scope is passed.
  5. session.refreshInterval is the lead time before expiry, not a polling
     interval; this is easy to misread.
Proposal: onRestore?: () => Promise<(Identity & { session? }) | null>, called
by the provider whenever the store holds no identity, and by refresh() when
there is none. Interim, works on 8.2.0: model restore as a variant of
authenticate(), e.g. authenticate({ kind: "restore" }).

extensions.asaidimu: 9.x and uses onRestore to adopt the cookie-backed session.

auth-20261029-005.title: logout() can leave client and IAM identity diverged; error-code check is dead
auth-20261029-005.body:
Resolved: logout() clears local identity in finally and treats an absent/expired session (NO_ACTIVE_SESSION/401) as success, so client and IAM cannot diverge on failure.

Any error other than "no active session" is rethrown BEFORE provider.clear(),
so a network blip leaves HestiaClient.store.identity set while IAM (which
clears first in deauthenticate) is already logged out, and callers that
stop the heartbeat after logout() skip that too.
err.code === "NO_ACTIVE_SESSION" never matches: DeleteSession returns
UNAUTHENTICATED with the message "no active session to revoke"; only the
substring check works. With an expired cookie the route (rule
authenticated) answers 401 before the handler runs, so that message is
never seen at all.
Fix: revoke best-effort, clear the local identity in a finally block, and
match on code/status rather than message text.

auth-20261029-006.title: authenticated() returns false without asking the server when local identity is null
auth-20261029-006.body:
Resolved: authenticated() asks the server via auth.session() when the local identity is null, keeping the apiKeyMode shortcut.

This is the direct cause of "every tab asks me to log in": a new tab has an
empty client store, so authenticated() answers false without a request even
though the HttpOnly cookie is valid. The name promises a server-confirmed
state but it only confirms when a local identity already exists.
Fix: once auth.session() exists (#auth-20261029-003) call it here
(null -> false, throw -> propagate), keeping the apiKeyMode shortcut. The
heartbeat is a poor probe because it carries no claims.

auth-20261029-007.title: onAuthStateChange has no unsubscribe and fires only on 401
auth-20261029-007.body:
Resolved: onAuthStateChange(cb) now returns an unsubscribe and is backed by store.watch("identity"), firing on login, logout, restore, refresh and 401 clears.

It now keeps a Set of callbacks, so several subscribers coexist, but it
returns nothing to unsubscribe and it fires only when a request gets 401,
not on login, logout or restore, despite the name. Consumers (the IAM
wrapper) therefore have to call back into their own provider to find out
what happened, and the client store and IAM store can drift.
Proposal: onAuthStateChange(cb: (identity: UserIdentity | null) => void):
() => void, backed by store.watch("identity"); keep 401 -> clear.

auth-20261029-008.title: Heartbeat lifecycle is hand-managed by every consumer, and it is what keeps the session alive
auth-20261029-008.body:
Resolved: HestiaClient watches store.identity and starts/stops the heartbeat automatically; autoHeartbeat:false plus start/stopHeartbeat remain as the opt-out.

Server session = 8h absolute (DefaultSessionTTL) with a 30min idle limit
(DefaultIdleTTL); any authenticated request after 15min (DefaultRefreshTTL)
re-issues the cookie, and NoRefreshCommands is never populated, so this
5min heartbeat is what makes access uninterrupted while a tab is open.
Consumers must start/stop it by hand (the IAM wrapper does so only inside
onAuthenticate/onDeauthenticate), so a restored session, an expiry-driven
logout or a cross-tab logout never starts/stops it.
Proposal: HestiaClient owns it, starting when store.identity becomes
non-null and stopping on null; keep start/stopHeartbeat as an opt-out.
Every tab runs its own timer (N tabs, N heartbeats): harmless, but could be
leader-elected. A suspended machine can exceed the idle limit; a re-login
there is expected behaviour, not a bug.

auth-20261029-009.title: No cross-tab auth signalling
auth-20261029-009.body:
Resolved: HestiaClient broadcasts only "changed" on hestia:auth:<baseUrl>; receivers re-run auth.session(). applyingRemoteAuth prevents ping-pong and claims are never broadcast.

Logout in tab A revokes the session id (blocklist) but tab B only learns at
its next heartbeat (up to 5 min) or 401. Login in tab A is never seen by
tab B. Proposal: post "changed" on a BroadcastChannel (name scoped to
baseUrl) after login/logout and, on receipt, re-run auth.session(). The
server stays the source of truth: never broadcast claims. Do not post from
the handler of a received message (ping-pong).

auth-20261029-010.title: Reference integration of HestiaClient with @asaidimu/iam 9.x
auth-20261029-010.body:
Resolved: reference integration updated to @asaidimu/iam 9.x (async factory, onRestore, refreshResult, onAuthChange mirroring HestiaClient).
Principle: the server's HttpOnly session cookie is the single source of
truth. IAM holds a copy of the claims for the UI, and every path that could
make that copy stale re-asks the server instead of trusting memory:
  - tab boot                 -> onRestore adopts an existing session
  - tab regains focus        -> refresh() re-validates and re-fetches claims
  - another tab logs in/out  -> HestiaClient BroadcastChannel -> auth.session()
  - any request gets a 401   -> HestiaClient clears identity -> IAM mirrors it
  - identity set or cleared  -> HestiaClient starts/stops the heartbeat

Requires @asaidimu/iam >= 9 (onRestore, async createAuthenticator,
refreshResult, refreshLeadTime) and HestiaAuth.session() on the client.
This file is not part of any package build.

extensions.asaidimu: 9.x (async factory, onRestore, refreshResult, onAuthChange mirroring HestiaClient).

Rate limiting is critical for HFT fair-use policies and IoT device

bench-20260821-002.title: Audit buffer needs throughput benchmarks
bench-20260821-002.body:
Audit logging is critical for compliance and security monitoring.
Current implementation lacks benchmarks for:

2. Buffer full behavior and fail-open performance
3. Memory usage with large entry sizes
4. Comparison with async vs sync persistence

blob-20261029-001.title: Upload sessions are not bound to the authorised namespace or to the principal that began them
blob-20261029-001.body:
Policy is resolved from arguments.ns (the NamespacedDispatcher rewrites system:blobs:blob:* to system:blobs:<ns>:*), but chunk, progress, abort and complete act on the session id alone. complete finalises into cu.NamespaceID/cu.Key, the others never compare the session's namespace with input.NS, and nothing records which principal ran begin. A caller allowed to complete (or abort, or write chunks) in namespace A can name a session id begun in namespace B, so the session id is the only capability. Not exercised by a test; verify before fixing.
Fix: store namespace (and principal) on the session at begin and reject any mismatch with NOT_FOUND, so a wrong id leaks nothing. See #blob-20261029-002 for the other complete-time hazard.

blob-20261029-002.title: complete without overwrite aborts the finished session and discards every uploaded byte
blob-20261029-002.body:
overwrite is a per-call modifier at begin AND at complete, and the session does not remember it. If begin ran with overwrite=true and complete omits it (or the key appeared in the meantime), ensureKeyWritable fails and this handler calls mgr.Abort(sessionID), deleting a possibly multi-GiB upload because of a flag mismatch.
Fix: persist overwrite on the session at begin and ignore the complete-time value; on ALREADY_EXISTS at complete leave the session intact so the caller can retry or rename. The client side of the same hazard is #blob-20261029-016.

blob-20261029-003.title: Blob downloads are served with only Content-Type, and that type is whatever the uploader declared
blob-20261029-003.body:
blobResponse sets Content-Type and nothing else: no X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, no Content-Disposition, no CSP sandbox. The stored type is client-supplied (BlobUploadInput.ContentType / begin content_type) and is never sniffed or allow-listed, and the client's blob(ns, key) hands out same-origin URLs. An uploader with write access can store text/html or image/svg+xml and get script running on the API origin inside a viewer's session (SameSite=Strict limits cross-site use, not same-site navigation). Not exercised; verify.
Also missing, for ergonomics: ETag/Last-Modified/Cache-Control and conditional requests, and Accept-Ranges/Range (no seeking in audio/video, no resumable downloads).
Fix: always send nosniff; default to Content-Disposition: attachment unless the type is on an inline allow-list (or a per-namespace setting); derive an ETag from the stored blob. Streaming is covered by #blob-20261029-004.

blob-20261029-004.title: Download buffers the whole blob; upload and chunk handlers copy their payloads
blob-20261029-004.body:
NewDownloadBlobHandler does Head then Get and io.ReadAll into abstract.Blob.Data, so memory per request equals the blob size, with no Range and no streaming. Resumable uploads can create blobs far beyond maxDirectUploadBytes (16 MiB), so a file that uploads fine can be impractical to read back. Head+Get is also two lookups, so the content type can describe a replaced body.
Related copies: NewUploadBlobHandler and NewUploadChunkHandler do append([]byte(nil), input.Payload...) before Release(), and a chunk may be up to 256 MiB (maxUploadChunkBytes), times the client's chunk concurrency (up to 6). Every system:blobs:* route also gets the large body limit (register.go, S-8), including JSON-only ones (list, update, begin, rename, namespace:create) that only need the small default.
serializeResponse answers a BlobChannel result with an empty 200, so a streaming blob result exists in the model but is not wired through HTTP. Proposal: stream downloads, honour Range, and apply the large limit only to upload and chunk. Header gaps are in #blob-20261029-003.

blob-20261029-005.title: Empty (zero-byte) blobs cannot be stored
blob-20261029-005.body:
NewUploadBlobHandler rejects len(payload) == 0 ("request body is required") and NewBeginUploadHandler rejects size <= 0, so neither path accepts an empty file (placeholders, .gitkeep, empty exports). The TS client sends every file at or below its 16 MiB threshold, including 0 bytes, down the direct path, so the caller just receives VALIDATION_ERROR.
Fix: accept empty bodies on the direct path (a missing body and an empty one are different things), or document the limit and fail early in the client. Related client behaviour: #blob-20261029-018.

blob-20261029-006.title: overwrite=false is check-then-put, so concurrent uploads to one key silently overwrite each other
blob-20261029-006.body:
ensureKeyWritable does Head, and the caller then does Put/PutCustom. Two requests that both see NOT_FOUND both succeed, the later one wins and neither receives ALREADY_EXISTS. The same applies at begin and again at complete (the repeated check narrows nothing). The contract "overwrite=false never replaces an existing blob" is therefore advisory under concurrency. Not exercised.
Fix: an atomic put-if-absent (or a per-key lock) in the store / blobs library. Complete-time behaviour is in #blob-20261029-002.

blob-20261029-007.title: List has no cursor, delimiter or truncation signal, and limit 0 returns everything
blob-20261029-007.body:
BlobListInput is {prefix, limit}; the store's List takes the same two values and the response is {blobs: [...]}. A namespace with many blobs comes back in one body, ordering is not specified here, and a caller who sets limit cannot tell whether more exist or fetch the next page. There is no delimiter either, so folder-style listings (keys containing '/') must download every key.
Proposal: opaque cursor in the request, next_cursor/has_more in BlobListDocument, an optional delimiter returning common_prefixes, and a server-side maximum limit. Client side of the same gap: #blob-20261029-021.

blob-20261029-008.title: No custom metadata can be attached at upload time
blob-20261029-008.body:
store.PutCustom and the completed staging upload both carry a Custom map (complete passes cu.Custom), but nothing populates it: BlobBeginInput and BlobUploadInput have no custom field, begin only hands the staging manager a content type, size and block size, and the client's UploadOptions has no custom either. Callers must upload and then call update() as a second, non-atomic step, and a failure in between leaves a blob without its metadata.
Proposal: accept payload.custom on begin and a custom form (query or header) on direct upload. The same gap exists for namespaces: #feat-ns-metadata.

blob-20261029-009.title: Namespace public flag lives in-band in custom, can be overridden by callers, and nothing enforces it
blob-20261029-009.body:
CreateNamespace writes custom["public"] = "true" and then copies the caller's custom map over it, so custom: {public: "false"} silently wins, and GetNamespace/ListNamespaces strip the key on read so a caller's own "public" key disappears. The flag is read back only for display: no code in core/ consults NamespaceView.Public to allow unauthenticated reads (grep found no other consumer), so "public" has no effect on access. The TS client does not expose it at all (#blob-20261029-026).
Also missing: system:blobs:namespace:get and :update routes. GetNamespace exists but is used only by the dispatcher hydrator, so clients list every namespace to read one and cannot change display_name, custom or public after creation (#feat-ns-metadata).
Fix: remove the flag, or give it a real field plus enforcement, and reject custom keys that collide with reserved ones.

blob-20261029-010.title: Namespace creation is not atomic and its id is barely validated
blob-20261029-010.body:
The steps are svc.CreateNamespace, SeedNamespaceBindings, RegisterBlobHandlers, with no rollback. A failure after the first leaves a namespace that exists but has no bindings or handlers, and retrying create then fails because it already exists, so it needs manual cleanup.
The id falls back to display_name when ns is empty and the only check is non-empty: spaces, ':' and '/' are accepted, and the ids "blob" or "namespace" produce per-namespace operation names (system:blobs:blob:*, system:blobs:namespace:list|stats|verify|delete) that collide with the static generic routes. Whether the blobs library itself rejects such ids was not verified.
Fix: validate ids (lowercase slug plus reserved words), drop the display_name fallback, and compensate (delete the namespace) on later failure. Deletion has the mirror problem: #blob-20261029-011.

blob-20261029-011.title: Namespace deletion destroys blobs without confirmation and can half-complete
blob-20261029-011.body:
Order is UnregisterBlobHandlers, delete each binding (returning on the first failure), ReloadPolicies, then svc.DeleteNamespace. A failure after the first step leaves a namespace that still holds data but has no handlers or bindings, and a namespace containing blobs is deleted outright: no emptiness check, no force or confirm flag, no soft delete.
Proposal: make each step idempotent so a retry converges, and require force=true for a non-empty namespace. Creation has the mirror problem: #blob-20261029-010.

blob-20261029-012.title: Inconsistent error model across blob operations
blob-20261029-012.body:
mapBlobError covers head, upload, download, update, delete, rename, stats, verify and compact, but list, namespace create/delete and begin wrap with fmt.Errorf (untyped, surfaced as an internal error), and the NamespacedDispatcher hydrator does the same for an unknown namespace. A mistyped namespace is therefore not NOT_FOUND, and the client's read(), which returns undefined only on code NOT_FOUND, throws instead.
Similar failures use different codes: VALIDATION_ERROR for bad parameters, INVALID_REQUEST for staging size/checksum/alignment problems. Some responses are ad hoc: rename answers {message: "renamed"} and verify {message: "ok"} with no declared output schema, so clients discard them, and verify offers no per-blob report (a CORRUPTION error is the only detail).
Fix: one mapper for blobs, staging and the hydrator, a short code table in docs/guide/blobs.md, and structured outputs (rename returns the BlobMeta, verify returns a report). Client side: #blob-20261029-025.

blob-20261029-013.title: blobOps, the static registrations and the dispatcher rewrite disagree
blob-20261029-013.body:
blobOps seeds a binding for "admin" but RegisterBlobHandlers registers no admin handler, so that binding is dead. "compact" has no per-namespace op at all. The NamespacedDispatcher rewrites only the system:blobs:blob: prefix, so system:blobs:namespace:stats|verify|compact (static, rule=root) appear never to consult the per-namespace stats/verify bindings that SeedNamespaceBindings creates; a non-root user granted <ns>:stats could not use the client's stats() (from reading, not exercised). compact is also registered with intent=create although it is a maintenance operation, and every binding is seeded as "root", so each grant is a manual policy edit.
Fix: make one op table the source of truth for registrations, bindings and rewrites.

blob-20261029-014.title: Resolved note claims delete triggers compaction, but no such call exists, and the note's body is lost
blob-20261029-014.body:
The note #storage-leak-blobs-never-compact-ad27adbb is marked resolved and says NewDeleteBlobHandler "now triggers async compaction after successful deletion". In this tree that handler only does Head and Delete, and the only caller of Compact is the root-only namespace:compact handler (grep over core/). Either compaction happens inside the blobs library or the fix was lost; stats().dead_bytes will show which.
Separately, that note has a directive line immediately followed by body text with no blank comment line, so under the devnotes grammar its entire body is silently discarded. Suggest re-verifying (and re-opening if needed) and adding the separator.

blob-20261029-015.title: Server limits are hard-coded and not discoverable by clients
blob-20261029-015.body:
maxDirectUploadBytes (16 MiB), the default and maximum block sizes, and the idle-session reaper window (store/service.go: StartReaper(5 min, 6 h)) are constants. The TS client hard-codes DEFAULT_DIRECT_THRESHOLD = 16 MiB and an 8 MiB block size to match, and a threshold set above the server limit fails with VALIDATION_ERROR. After a session is reaped, progress() answers NOT_FOUND and ResumableUpload.run() ends in "error" with no attempt to begin a fresh session.
Proposal: make the limits configuration, return them from begin (or a small capabilities route), and let the client restart on a NOT_FOUND session while the File is still available. See #blob-20261029-018 for the client's direct-path handling.

blob-20261029-016.title: Restored uploads lose overwrite and other options, and can be discarded at completion
blob-20261029-016.body:
restoreAsync rebuilds each job with options { key, contentType: snap.type, overwrite: false }. UploadJobSnapshot persists neither overwrite, nor a caller's contentType override, nor anything else from UploadOptions. An upload started with overwrite: true and then resumed completes with overwrite: false; if the key exists the server answers ALREADY_EXISTS and aborts the session, discarding everything uploaded (#blob-20261029-002).
Fix: persist the serialisable options (not onProgress/signal) in the snapshot and restore them, and let restoreAsync take per-job option overrides. The sibling stub is #blob-20261029-017.

blob-20261029-017.title: UploadQueue.restore() is a stub that always returns an empty array
blob-20261029-017.body:
restore() reads the persistence, discards the result and returns []. Only restoreAsync() works, and the name and doc comment suggest otherwise. Restored jobs are added to jobs but not to queue and get no onStatusChange hook, so they bypass the maxConcurrent accounting that enqueue() sets up, and snapshots with no File and no fileProvider result are skipped silently and stay in persistence forever.
Fix: delete restore() (or make it throw), route restored jobs through the same wiring as enqueue(), and report or clean unrestorable snapshots. Lost options are in #blob-20261029-016.

blob-20261029-018.title: onProgress, signal and retries are silently ignored for files at or below the direct threshold
blob-20261029-018.body:
upload() sends files up to the threshold (default 16 MiB) through uploadDirect, which honours only contentType and overwrite. onProgress is never called (not even once at 100%), signal cannot abort the request, and retries, concurrency and blockSize are ignored. Most uploads are small, so most callers get neither progress nor cancel.
Fix: pass signal to dispatch, report progress (or at least a final 100%), retry transient failures, and expose which path was used. Server-side constraints on this path: #blob-20261029-005 and #blob-20261029-015.

blob-20261029-019.title: upload() requires options.key at runtime but types it as optional
blob-20261029-019.body: upload({ file, options }) throws "options.key is required" although UploadOptions.key is optional; the value is cast with `as string` in upload(), createUpload() and UploadQueue.enqueue(). Proposal: upload(key, file, options), or default the key to file.name, and make the type say so. The return type Promise<Document | undefined> is explained in #blob-20261029-020.

blob-20261029-020.title: done resolves undefined on cancel, and failures can surface as unhandled rejections
blob-20261029-020.body:
finishCancelled() resolves done with undefined, so Promise<Document | undefined> mixes "cancelled" with success, and callers must test for undefined with nothing telling them it means cancellation (an aborted AbortSignal would normally reject with AbortError). Conversely run() calls rejectDone on failure while UploadQueue.enqueue() never attaches a handler, so when nobody reads done a failed upload raises an unhandledrejection; after retry() the earlier rejected promise is replaced and stays unhandled.
Fix: reject with AbortError on cancel, and attach a no-op catch inside the class (callers that await done still see the rejection). Related signature issue: #blob-20261029-019.

blob-20261029-021.title: find()/list() fabricate paging metadata and mostly ignore the query
blob-20261029-021.body:
pageMeta() reports number 1, pages 1 and total = items.length for any result, so with a limit set the pager cannot tell that more exist. QueryDSL<BlobMeta> filters and sorts are ignored: only (query as any).prefix and limit are read, so list({ prefix }) does not type-check without a cast and a filter silently returns everything. setPrefix() is mutable instance state that overrides a prefix passed in the call, and because HestiaBlobClient.namespace() returns a new BlobNamespace each time (#blob-20261029-023) that state is easily lost.
Fix: accept ListBlobsRequest ({ prefix, limit, cursor }) in list(), fill paging from the server's cursor (#blob-20261029-007), and build the pager lazily.

blob-20261029-022.title: update() cannot do what its type says
blob-20261029-022.body:
update takes Partial<BlobMeta> but sends { custom: strippedData(data) }, and strippedData removes only _id_ and _metadata_. So update({ data: { content_type: "text/plain" } }) sends {"custom":{"content_type":"text/plain"}}, writing a custom key named content_type instead of changing the type, and a correctly typed update({ data: { custom: { owner: "a" } } }) sends {"custom":{"custom":{"owner":"a"}}}, which the server (Custom map[string]string; UpdateMetadata persists only custom) rejects or mangles. Payload shapes were reproduced in a script; not run against a server. The existing test (blobs.test.ts) asserts the first shape as if it worked.
Fix: update({ id, custom }) with string-only values; the type drift behind this is in #blob-20261029-026.

blob-20261029-023.title: Instance and naming semantics of HestiaBlobClient
blob-20261029-023.body:
blob(ns, key) returns a URL string, not a blob or handle (url() would say so). apiPrefix is accepted and stored but never used. namespace() returns a new BlobNamespace on every call, so queue() called twice yields two independent queues and maxConcurrent is not global, and queue(options) silently ignores options after the first call on an instance; each BlobNamespace also builds a ReactiveDataStore and pager in its constructor even if page() is never used.
Fix: cache namespaces by name (or document that they are cheap handles), reject conflicting queue options, and build the pager lazily. Effect on prefix state: #blob-20261029-021.

blob-20261029-024.title: BlobNamespace implements DocumentStore but several members throw
blob-20261029-024.body:
create, subscribe, notify and stream throw "not supported" at runtime, and update rejects filter. Generic UI code typed against DocumentStore compiles and then fails on first call, and the capability gap is not visible in the types. asDoc() also invents document metadata: _id_ is the bare key (not namespace-qualified), _metadata_.checksum is "" and version is always 1.
Fix: narrow to a capability interface that blobs satisfy honestly, or implement subscribe through polling or server events; drop the fabricated metadata or mark it as synthetic.

blob-20261029-025.title: delete, rename, verify and namespace calls return nothing useful
blob-20261029-025.body:
delete() is Head + Delete on the server, so deleting an absent key fails with NOT_FOUND (not idempotent) and costs two lookups. rename() returns void although the server knows the new key, has no overwrite control, and answers {message} (#blob-20261029-012). verify() returns void. createNamespace() cannot send public (#blob-20261029-009) and deleteNamespace() has no force flag.
Fix: idempotent delete (or an ignoreMissing option), rename returning the BlobDocument, verify returning a report.

blob-20261029-026.title: Naming and typing drift between client and server
blob-20261029-026.body:
One concept, three spellings: ns (CreateNamespaceRequest, route arguments), id (NamespaceInfo), namespace_id (BlobMeta, NamespaceStats). NamespaceInfo.custom is Record<string, string> but BlobMeta.custom is Record<string, any>, while the server uses map[string]string for both (#blob-20261029-022 shows the consequence). NamespaceInfo and CreateNamespaceRequest lack the server's public field (#blob-20261029-009). BlobMeta timestamps are strings while Document metadata uses created/updated, and UploadJobSnapshot.name/type duplicate the File.
Fix: one spelling per concept, and generate these types from the server schemas, which are already derived with SchemaFromType.

mem-20260821-003.title: Stream channel buffer size causes goroutine leaks
mem-20260821-003.body:
selects on the request context while draining the source channel and while
forwarding to the response stream, so on client disconnect the producer
returns instead of blocking forever on a full buffer. S-19 additionally
verified fasthttp's RequestCtx.Done() never fires on client disconnect
(server-shutdown only) and moved SSE teardown to managedStream, whose
writer-owned done channel releases the producer on flush error or stream
end — the transport, not the request context, owns stream shutdown.

streamChannel (line 171) creates a channel with buffer size 64. If the
consumer stops reading (e.g., client disconnects), the producer goroutine
blocks indefinitely, causing a goroutine leak.

For IoT/HFT:
- IoT devices may disconnect frequently
- HFT systems need clean resource management
- Goroutine leaks accumulate over time

Resolution:
1. Use a select with context cancellation when sending
2. Add a timeout or context to the producer goroutine
3. Consider using a bounded buffer with overflow handling
4. Monitor goroutine count for leak detection
managedStream pairs the SSE body channel with a done channel that the
fasthttp response writer owns. The producer cannot rely on the request
context alone: fasthttp's RequestCtx.Done() returns the server-shutdown
channel (server.go: ctx.s.done) and never fires on client disconnect —
without the writer-owned done channel, every aborted SSE request leaked
the producer goroutine and its upstream subscription until server
shutdown (S-19).

perf-20260821-001.title: Request struct has poor field ordering
perf-20260821-001.body:
Request struct (line 9) has suboptimal field ordering for memory alignment:

Current layout (64-bit):
- Operation: string (16 bytes)
- Body: []byte (24 bytes)
- PathParams: map (8 bytes)
- Query: map (8 bytes)
- Headers: map (8 bytes)
- Cookies: map (8 bytes)
- ClientIP: string (16 bytes)
- UserAgent: string (16 bytes)
- RequestID: string (16 bytes)

Total: ~120 bytes with possible padding

Better ordering (group by size):
- Body: []byte (24 bytes)
- Operation: string (16 bytes)
- ClientIP: string (16 bytes)
- UserAgent: string (16 bytes)
- RequestID: string (16 bytes)
- PathParams: map (8 bytes)
- Query: map (8 bytes)
- Headers: map (8 bytes)
- Cookies: map (8 bytes)

For IoT/HFT: Every byte matters on memory-constrained devices.
This struct is created for every HTTP request.

Resolution: Reorder fields to minimize padding. Consider using a pool
for Request objects to reduce allocations.

perf-20260821-002.title: Response struct has mixed pointer/value types
perf-20260821-002.body:
Response struct (line 42) mixes pointer and value types inefficiently:

- Status: int (8 bytes)
- Headers: map (8 bytes)
- Body: any (16 bytes - interface)
- Cookies: []Cookie (24 bytes - slice)
- Page: *query.PaginationInfo (8 bytes - pointer)
- Metadata: map (8 bytes)

The Body field is an interface, which means it can hold any type.
This causes boxing/unboxing overhead and prevents compiler optimizations.

For IoT/HFT: Interface types cause GC pressure and prevent inlining.

Resolution:
1. Consider using concrete types instead of interface{} for Body
2. Group pointer types together to minimize padding
3. Consider using a pool for Response objects

perf-20260821-003.title: trieNode uses slice for children
perf-20260821-003.body:
trieNode struct (line 8) uses a slice for children:

- segment: string (16 bytes)
- children: []*trieNode (24 bytes - slice)
- paramChild: *trieNode (8 bytes)
- paramName: string (16 bytes)
- handlers: map (8 bytes)

Most trie nodes have 1-2 children. Using a slice causes:
1. Heap allocation for the slice header
2. Indirection for each child access
3. GC pressure from small allocations

For IoT/HFT: Route lookup is on the hot path for every request.

Resolution:
1. Use [2]*trieNode for small child counts with fallback to slice
2. Or use a fixed-size array with linear search for 1-2 children
3. Consider embedding the first child inline

perf-20260821-004.title: BuildInputDocument uses unnecessary JSON round-trip
perf-20260821-004.body:
BuildInputDocument manually constructs a JSON string by marshaling each
field, concatenating into a JSON object, then parsing it back into a
document via pool.FromJSON. This is:

1. Wasteful: marshal Go values → JSON bytes → concatenate → parse JSON
2. Incorrect for bytes: json.Marshal([]byte) base64-encodes, double-encoding
3. Error-prone: manual JSON construction can produce invalid JSON

The anansi Document has direct Set* methods:

     doc, _ := pool.New()
     doc.SetString("arguments.name", value)
     doc.SetBytes("payload", req.Body)

This should populate fields directly without JSON:
 1. pool.New() to get an empty document
 2. For context: iterate input.ContextFields(), set each from req.Headers
    via contextHeaderCandidates
 3. For arguments: iterate input.Arguments(), set each from req.PathParams
 4. For modifiers: iterate input.Modifiers(), set each from req.Query
 5. For payload: if bytes, doc.SetBytes(); if JSON, use DecodeJSONField

Note: Do NOT duplicate JSON decode logic. The anansi decoder (go-anansi/
core/encoding/json) is already optimized. Use DecodeJSONField for JSON
payloads — it decodes a single field directly into the document without
building an intermediate JSON object.

Impact:
- Eliminates marshal/parse round-trip (2x CPU savings)
- Eliminates base64 encoding for byte payloads (33% memory savings)
- Eliminates intermediate JSON buffer allocation
- For IoT/HFT: Critical for reducing per-request latency

Resolution: Rewrite BuildInputDocument to use pool.New() and doc.Set*()
methods directly, using DecodeJSONField only for JSON payload types.
contextHeaderCandidates returns the deterministic candidate list for
lifting a declared context field from request headers, most specific
standard form first: "content_type" → ["Content-Type", "X-Content-Type"].
The standard spelling wins when a client supplies both; the X-prefixed
form covers custom transport headers like X-Session-ID. Matching is done
case-insensitively by requestHeaderValue.

review2-20260821-001.title: SessionService.Validate does not check ExpiresAt
review2-20260821-001.body: Validate() cryptographically verifies the HMAC and decodes the payload, but never compares ExpiresAt against time.Now(). Expiry is only enforced by callers that happen to re-check info.ExpiresAt after calling ValidateSession -- the HTTP middleware (core/interface/http/middleware.go) does this correctly, but utils/wails/dispatch.go has at least two call sites (around the post-login and dispatch-response handling paths) that call CredProvider.ValidateSession and consume the result without checking ExpiresAt at all. A method literally named Validate should be the single source of truth for token validity, including expiry; relying on every caller to remember a manual time check is fragile and has already produced inconsistent enforcement across call sites. review2-20260821-002.title: ValidateSession result used without checking ExpiresAt
review2-20260821-002.body: Two call sites in this file (around line 122, in the post-login flow, and here around line 245-251, in dispatch response handling) consume the ValidateSession result and set a.userID/a.claims without checking info.ExpiresAt. Contrast with the correctly-guarded call sites at lines 163-167, 179-182, and 382-395 in this same file, which all check info.ExpiresAt > time.Now().Unix() before trusting the claims. The line-122 case is low risk in practice (it runs immediately after a fresh login, so the token cannot yet be expired), but the line-245 case handles an arbitrary dispatch response and has no such guarantee. review2-20260821-004.title: system:updates:check:create conflates checking with staging (and a fleet cannot poll safely)
review2-20260821-004.body:
RESOLVED 2026-08-22: split into system:updates:check:get (read-only
availability) and system:updates:stage:create (download+prepare+notify);
check:create kept as the backward-compatible check-then-stage wrapper and
RunScheduledCheck still drives both effects back to back via checkAndStage.

Despite the doc comment calling this "the read-only check", Check() always
calls checkAndStage() (below), which both checks for a new version AND
downloads + prepares it via s.updater.PrepareUpdate whenever one is found.
There is no way to ask "is a newer version available" without triggering a
download and disk write. The registered message name itself says
"check:create" (Intent: abstract.Create) rather than a Read intent, which
is the tell -- this was never actually a read operation.

This is a real problem for a P2P/fleet deployment, not just a naming
nit: a coordinator that wants to poll version availability across N nodes
(e.g. before deciding whether to trigger a staged rollout) cannot do so
without every node downloading the update artifact, even nodes that won't
end up applying it. At fleet scale that's N redundant downloads for a
single availability check, and it removes the option of a lightweight
"any updates available?" health-check message that's safe to poll on a
short interval.

Resolution: split into two messages/methods:
  - system:updates:check:get (Read) -> calls only s.updater.CheckForUpdate,
    returns {Available bool, Version string} with no side effects.
  - system:updates:stage:create (Create) -> calls PrepareUpdate, keeping
    today's staging + notify-admins behavior.

Check() (or a thin wrapper) can still exist for backward compatibility,
calling both in sequence, but the two effects should be independently
callable. RunScheduledCheck can keep calling both back to back since a
cron job doing its own check-then-stage is the correct behavior there.

Check runs the read-only check, stages a newer version when available, and
notifies admins when a release was newly staged. With AutoApply it applies
immediately (the process exits on success). Kept for backward
compatibility; prefer system:updates:check:get +
system:updates:stage:create so each effect stays independently callable.

@hestia.register(

	name="system:updates:check:create",
	intent="create",
	rule="root",
	description="Check for and stage an update (legacy check-then-stage)",
	output="CheckView",

)

review2-20260821-005.title: Dispatcher.Send is synchronous end-to-end with no async/remote-capable variant
review2-20260821-005.body:
Every implementation in the chain -- LocalDispatcher, SecureDispatcher,
RateLimitDispatcher, AuditLog/TenantDispatcher, RecoveryDispatcher,
BootstrapDispatcher -- wraps the next Dispatcher and calls Send() as a
direct, blocking Go function call that returns (*Result, error) on the
same goroutine. LocalDispatcher.Send (core/runtime/local-dispatcher.go:52)
is the base case: it does `return entry.fn(msg.Context(), msg)` with no
queue, no channel handoff, and no notion of "this might take a network
round-trip." Every transport (HTTP, CLI, Wails) calls Dispatcher.Send and
blocks the calling goroutine until it returns.

This is fine for a single-process monolith (net/http already gives you
per-request concurrency via goroutines, so throughput isn't the problem)
but it is the central architectural blocker for the P2P node deployment
goal: there is currently no seam where a message could be routed to a
*different* node instead of a local handler. Adding that seam later
without an async story means either (a) blocking a goroutine per in-flight
remote call indefinitely, or (b) a breaking change to this interface.

Resolution -- concretely, in order of increasing scope:
 1. Add a context.Context parameter to Send itself: Send(ctx, msg) instead
    of relying on msg.Context(). This is a prerequisite for #2 and #3
    because a remote dispatcher needs the caller's ctx for cancellation/
    deadline propagation independent of what's embedded in the message.
 2. Introduce a second interface alongside Dispatcher, not a replacement:
    type AsyncDispatcher interface {
    SendAsync(ctx context.Context, msg Message) (<-chan Result, error)
    }
    LocalDispatcher can implement this trivially by running entry.fn in a
    goroutine and writing to a buffered chan of size 1. A future
    RemoteDispatcher (or P2PDispatcher) implements the same interface by
    serializing msg, publishing it over the network transport, and
    resolving the channel when a correlated response arrives (or the ctx
    deadline fires). Existing synchronous callers are unaffected; new
    transports (or existing ones once ready) adopt SendAsync incrementally.
 3. Every DispatcherLink.Wrap in the chain needs an Async-aware equivalent
    so cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate-limit, audit, tenant scoping)
    still apply uniformly whether the terminal handler is local or remote.
    Concretely: change DispatcherLink.Wrap to operate on the AsyncDispatcher
    interface, and provide a `SyncFromAsync` adapter (blocks and unwraps
    the channel) so the existing Dispatcher call sites in HTTP/CLI/Wails
    don't all need to change on day one.
 4. Message routing needs an explicit locality concept before any of this
    is useful: something has to decide "is this message's target handler
    local to this node, or does it need to go over the wire to node X".
    abstract.Message today has no notion of a target node/peer -- TenantID
    is the closest thing, and tenant != node. This is a bigger design
    question (service discovery / handler advertisement across the mesh)
    that should be settled before committing to the exact shape of #2.

scheduled-dispatch-errors-are-sw-616004c.title: Scheduled dispatch errors are swallowed by the cron chain
scheduled-dispatch-errors-are-sw-616004c.body: LiveSchedule.dispatch returns errors from dispatch.Await, but robfig/cron only logs panics (Recover wrapper) — returned errors vanish silently. A broken schedule (e.g. unregistered message, DTO binding failure) ticks forever with no trace. While fixing the payload-envelope bug (input must be wrapped in {"payload": ...} to satisfy input:"payload.*" DTO bindings, same as core/interface/cli/orchestrator.go does) this cost significant debugging time on the live server. Consider logging dispatch failures via ls.log in dispatch(), or a cron.PrintfLogger chain.

sec-20260821-003.title: No rate limiting on authentication attempts
sec-20260821-003.body:
Resolved (S-3, security batch 1): authMiddleware throttles unauthenticated
authentication attempts per source IP through authRateLimiter (a shared
ratestore) via CheckAndConsume with authRateLimitBurst/authRateLimitPeriod
before any credential validation runs; once the bucket is empty the
request is rejected with 429. The gate covers the credential-carrying
messages listed in authRateLimitedMessages (login, elevate, confirm, ...).
The per-operation RateLimitPolicy on the dispatch path remains the second
layer (see the ratelimit dispatcher link).

storage-leak-blobs-never-compact-ad27adb.title: Storage leak: blobs never compacted after deletion
storage-leak-blobs-never-compact-ad27adb.body:
When blobs or namespaces are deleted via system:blobs:blob:delete or system:blobs:namespace:delete,
the physical segment files (.vol, .wal) remain on disk because Compact is never called.
The blob library (github.com/asaidimu/blobs) relies on Compact to reclaim space from deleted chunks.
Need to either: 1) call Compact after bulk deletions, 2) add a background compaction job, or 3) expose Compact via API for operators.

update-hash-verify.title: Verify binary hash before applying staged update
update-hash-verify.body:
The staged binary at DataDir/update is copied over the running executable
(swapExecutable) or executed directly (ApplyUpdate) without verifying its
SHA-256 checksum against UpdateInfo.Checksum. The Checksum field already

S-9 residual (authenticity): a self-computed checksum is integrity-only.
The GitHub provider supplies no checksum, so the recorded value attests
nothing about provenance — a MITM-substituted binary passes by
construction. Full remediation requires provider-attested checksums or
signed releases verified against an out-of-band-pinned key (updater's
server provider already verifies RSA signatures when ServerPublicKey is
configured).
flows through the persistence layer, but the actual verification against
the on-disk binary is never performed. This means a corrupted download —
or a file tampered with between staging and apply — would silently replace
the running binary. The check should re-hash the staged file and abort
the swap/exec if it does not match.

Real-world hit: /opt/hedwig-server/hedwig-server ended up as an ELF with
"missing section headers" — the update was applied but the binary was
corrupted. A pre-apply hash check would have caught this.

Why staging can succeed while application produces a corrupted binary:
  1. GitHub provider passes empty checksum (github.go:133) so
     DownloadBinary skips hash verification entirely.
  2. Neither copyFile (process.go:62) nor swapExecutable (service.go:301)
     re-hash the staged file before overwriting the executable.
  3. copyFile does io.Copy + Sync but a mid-copy I/O error or disk-full
     condition can leave the destination truncated.
  4. swapExecutable creates a temp file in filepath.Dir(exe) which may
     differ from DataDir — if they share a filesystem the Rename is
     atomic, but a failed copy to the temp file is not caught before the
     rename.

@see #updater-hash-verify

tool-20261029-006.title: Two config files describe overlapping layout and nothing checks they agree
tool-20261029-006.body:
hestia.json (module, core_dir, modules_dir, autogen, commands) and anansi.json (schema.glob, lockfile, migrations_dir, tsgen.out, gogen, metadata) both encode where things live, for example whether the schema glob covers core_dir and modules_dir, and where migrations go (#tool-20261029-005).
Options: keep both files but derive anansi defaults from hestia.json when keys are absent and report disagreement; or accept an "anansi" section in hestia.json while still honouring anansi.json for standalone use (precedence: explicit anansi.json, then the hestia.json section, then derived defaults). Avoid a third file or flag-only configuration. Depends on the embedding in #tool-20261029-001.

tool-20261029-002.title: No single command runs the whole schema-to-service pipeline
tool-20261029-002.body:
After a schema change the documented sequence (README, skills/SKILL.md) is: anansi migrate generate --dry-run, anansi migrate generate, anansi codegen golang, then hestia generate modules and hestia service generate <module> <name> for each affected service. Order matters (models before service registrations) and each step is a different tool with its own config.
Proposal: `hestia sync` = migrate generate, then codegen golang (and typescript when configured), then service generate for every service, then generate modules. Flags: --dry-run, and --check that exits non-zero when anything would change (anansi already has --check for migrations) so CI can gate on it, plus one summary of changed files. The individual verbs stay available once embedded (#tool-20261029-001). Option drift between generators is #tool-20261029-003.

tool-20261029-004.title: init does not make the project anansi-ready
tool-20261029-004.body:
init writes main.go, the Makefile, .env, .gitignore and hestia.json, but no anansi.json, schemas directory or lockfile. A fresh project cannot run migrate or codegen until the user runs `anansi scaffold --existing` separately, and anansi's default glob would not match hestia's core_dir/modules_dir layout.
Fix: once scaffold is importable (#tool-20261029-001), have init create anansi.json non-destructively, with the glob derived from core_dir and modules_dir, and add sync/check targets to the generated Makefile. Config overlap is #tool-20261029-006.

tool-20261029-005.title: Per-module model/migrations directories are scaffolded but nothing populates them
tool-20261029-005.body:
This (and `service new --model` in service.go) creates <module>/model/migrations, but anansi's config has a single schema.migrations_dir and lockfile, and hestia's own repo keeps all 16 migrations in core/internal/migrations (there are no per-service model/migrations directories). The scaffolded directories stay empty and imply a per-module layout the tooling cannot produce, since one run emits into one directory.
Decide: (a) a project-level migrations directory and drop this scaffolding, or (b) teach anansi per-schema output (for example a schema-relative migrations_dir) so each module owns its migrations and lockfile entries. (b) matters if modules are meant to ship independently. Related config question: #tool-20261029-006.

tool-20261029-003.title: service new and anansi codegen write the same *.model.go with different options
tool-20261029-003.body:
generateModel (used by `service new --model`) builds golang.GeneratorConfig from fixed values: PackageName "model", NameRules ^_(.+)_$ -> System (hestia's own convention for _user_-style system schemas), DefaultTagConfig, no Mode and no ScopedPackages. `anansi codegen golang` (RunGoGen) reads tags, scoped, name_rules and mode from anansi.json, derives the package name from the directory, and writes the same <schema>.model.go next to the schema.
With a non-default anansi.json the next codegen run rewrites what service new produced (churn, possibly different type names), and user projects inherit the System rule meant for hestia's own schemas. Fix: one entry point (the embedded codegen, #tool-20261029-001) driven by the project's config (#tool-20261029-006); service new should call it for just that schema.

tool-20261029-001.title: hestia cannot embed the anansi CLI because its logic is unimportable
tool-20261029-001.body:
anansi's commands live in go-anansi cmd/anansi/main.go (package main) and cmd/anansi/internal (schema new/normalize, migrate generate/squash, codegen golang/typescript/faker, scaffold, agents). Go forbids importing either from another module, so hestia can only call the public libraries it already uses (codegen/golang). Every other step is a separate binary: README and skills/SKILL.md tell users to run `anansi migrate generate --dry-run`, `anansi migrate generate` and `anansi codegen golang` by hand, then hestia's own generators (#tool-20261029-002).
Version drift: go.mod pins go-anansi v8.10.1 (latest tag is v8.10.2) while the CLI is installed independently, and the migration and model output depends on the CLI version that happened to run.
End state: in go-anansi, move command construction out of main/internal into an importable package (for example .../cli returning the schema, migrate, codegen and agents cobra commands, taking the config location and writers), keep cmd/anansi as a thin main, and mount them in hestia (hestia schema|migrate|codegen|agents) so the binary is version-locked to go.mod. The logic already depends only on public packages (core/schema/definition, core/data, codegen/*, skills/anansi).
Interim, no upstream change (not exercised): add `tool github.com/asaidimu/go-anansi/v8/cmd/anansi` to go.mod (this module is on Go 1.27) and make a hestia passthrough run `go tool anansi`. Do not exec whatever `anansi` is on PATH.
Skills: `hestia agents` should install both the hestia and anansi skills; skills/SKILL.md currently says "see the anansi skill". Follow-ups: #tool-20261029-003 and #tool-20261029-004.

err-20261103-4.title: SDK drops server-sent error details
err-20261103-4.body:
The server serializes failures as { error: { code, message, details } }
with details carrying issue.Cause for 4xx (transport_fasthttp.go
writeError), but this parser only reads body.details?.issues - so
validation causes and policy-denial details sent by the server never reach
SDK callers. Align this shape with the wire format, or make the server
emit details.issues.

err-20261103-5.title: Panic response body omits the request ID
err-20261103-5.body:
This canned body has no metadata.request, so panic responses
break the request-ID correlation every other error path
maintains (the X-Request-ID response header from
correlationID is still set).

err-20261103-7.title: Error-reporting topology for a failed API call
err-20261103-7.body:
A failed call is classified in writeError. A *common.SystemError maps to a
status via codeToStatusFn and keeps issue.Cause as `details` for 4xx; any
other error becomes an opaque 500 whose cause is logged server-side only.
Every path is correlated by X-Request-ID (generated in correlationID,
echoed in the response header and metadata.request); the same ID lands in
the zap log lines and audit entries. Handler errors that reach the audit
link store the full error string in the audit collection (status=error,
indexed by request_id); denials and limiter rejections never reach it.

err-20261103-1.title: Non-SystemError handler failures surface as an opaque 500
err-20261103-1.body:
The default branch replaces any error that is not a *common.SystemError
with INTERNAL_ERROR / "internal server error" (S-16: raw strings must not
reach clients). Most feature handlers return plain wrapped errors (e.g.
fmt.Errorf("create document in %q: %w", ...)), so the common failure path
gives clients nothing to act on and pushes all diagnosis onto the log
file. Fix direction: make handlers return SystemErrors with causes
(WithCause) so 4xx details reach clients and 5xx causes are classifiable,
rather than widening what leaks across the wire.

err-20261103-2.title: A 5xx SystemError's cause may be logged nowhere
err-20261103-2.body:
The errors.As branch strips details for status >= 500 (S-16, correct),
but this Warn records only issue.Message - the Error-level "internal
error" log fires only in the default branch. A SystemError carrying a
WithCause chain whose code maps to 5xx therefore has its root cause in
neither the response nor the transport log; only the audit record may
still hold the full error string.

err-20261103-6.title: Collections are not "schema-less", docs say otherwise
err-20261103-6.body:
Collection creation requires a valid Anansi schema (checked here and
with ValidateSchema below), so runtime collections are
runtime-declared schemas, not schema-less. README.md ("schema-less
document CRUD, like Firestore") and skills/SKILL.md use the
misleading term; "dynamic schema" / "schema-flexible" is accurate
and avoids inviting users who expect zero validation.

err-20261103-3.title: Authorization and limiter denials never reach the audit collection
err-20261103-3.body:
The audit link sits innermost, so secure/ratelimit/throttle rejections
short-circuit before it and are recorded only as Warn lines in the zap
log, not in the queryable audit store. SecureDispatcher has no logger of
its own either. Moving audit above secure, or adding a dedicated denial
audit path, would close the compliance gap the platform guide already
flags (skills/references/platform-guide.md).
